https://www.dw.com/en/hurricane-isaias-m.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O5sS Isaias brings the risk of flooding to low-lying areas of Florida's Gulf coast Image: Chris Urso/REUTERS Advertisement Hurricane Isaias has made landfall as a Category 2 storm near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Friday evening. Destin is in the panhandle region of northern Florida. What do we know about Hurricane Isaias? The NHC warned of "life-threatening storm surge impacting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland." The weather system is also bringing extreme winds, with a tornado watch issued for parts of Florida and southern Georgia. Isaias is packing sustained winds of up to 105 miles per hour Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP After the storm made landfall, the Florida Division of Emergency Management said the tornado watch for parts of North Florida has been extended until at least 6 a.m. local time Saturday (10 a.m. UTC). The NHC said the hurricane has maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (165 kilometers per hour). The storm is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season and was originally a strong Category 3 storm before making landfall. It is expected to weaken as it passes over land. The storm has downed trees in Pensacola in the Florida panhandle Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP Evacuations took place in coastal communities as the hurricane approached. Florida, Georgia and Alabama have all declared a State of Emergency due to the extreme weather system. US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said "emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to #Isaias." Florida Governor DeSantis urges residents to 'buckle down' In a press conference, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis urged residents to "buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads." Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned those "thinking about using this storm's power outages and evacuations to break in, loot, or steal: don't even try it." "During an emergency, these crimes become first-degree felonies, punishable by up to 30 years in prison," Uthmeier said. People boarded up businesses ahead of the storm's landfall Image: Marco Bello/REUTERS According to power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, roughly 480,000 customers altogether were without electricity as of Friday evening in Florida, Georgia and Alabama. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said Uber, Comcast and Home Depot have offered to help Alabamians during the storm. Uber, for example, is offering free round-trip rides to state-approved evacuation shelters in Mobile and Baldwin counties. http://www.bgnes.com/entertainment/mike-.text: Legendary American actor Stacey Keach, best known for playing private detective Mike Hammer in the television series of the same name, but also widely regarded as an outstanding interpreter of Shakespeare, has died aged 85, The Independent reports. Keach died at his home in Magdalenka, Poland, ‘after a long and hard-fought battle with serious heart disease and congestive heart failure’, his wife, Polish actress Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. The actor had previously survived a heart attack suffered on stage during a one-man performance in Chicago in June 2017. A varied career on stage and screen Keach was one of the most respected theatre actors in the United States and a favourite of directors such as John Huston. In popular culture, however, he remained best known for his portrayal of Mike Hammer, the tough, hard-boiled television private detective created by crime writer Mickey Spillane. Yet Keach was reluctant to be typecast and constantly sought out different roles. He played a ‘hippie cop’ on screen, took on the role of King Lear on stage, narrated the television series World’s Most Amazing Videos, portrayed a deranged colonel in The Ninth Configuration, starred in the series Titus and appeared in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska. Last year, he also played the embittered father of George Clooney’s character in Jay Kelly. ‘My aim was to have as wide a variety of roles as possible. That probably hurt my career, but my choices came at a price. Still, I played Hamlet, Richard III and King Lear – and I wouldn’t trade that for anything in the world,’ he told New York Magazine in 2012. His major screen and stage roles included the French artist Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries Mistral’s Daughter, a Russian prince in the adaptation of Judith Krantz’s novel Princess Daisy, Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli’s Jesus of Nazareth and Major Jonas Steele in The Blue and the Gray. He won a Golden Globe for his portrayal of Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour television miniseries, a role for which he gained 16kg. Keach also received a Tony Award nomination for playing Buffalo Bill in the Broadway production of Indians. He appeared as King Lear on Broadway alongside Lee J. Cobb and later performed in The Kentucky Cycle, The Country Wife and Other Desert Cities. He toured nationally as the disgraced president in Frost/Nixon and also appeared in Sleuth. In 2006, he played King Lear at Chicago’s Goodman Theatre. It was there, in 2017, that he collapsed on stage during Pamplona, a one-man play about Hemingway. The arrest that nearly destroyed his career While filming Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer, Keach was arrested at London’s Heathrow Airport in 1984. Police found 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol can of shaving cream and elsewhere in his luggage. His secretary was also arrested. ‘When they read out my sentence – nine months in prison – I felt as though someone had kicked me in the groin with lead boots,’ he later wrote in his 2013 autobiography, All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage. ‘It was the lowest point of my life.’ The actor, then 44, was led away in handcuffs and sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security facility, because the authorities believed that a minimum-security prison would make it too easy for journalists to gain access to him. He was released after six months. Keach later recalled receiving warm letters of support in prison from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He described the experience as ‘very lonely, very depressing, very sad’ – a period spent ‘re-evaluating my own stupidity’. After his release, Keach appeared in the television documentary series High on the Job. He also gave evidence at a congressional hearing, describing how he had become addicted to cocaine in the mid-1970s. ‘There is no greater prison than being dependent on a chemical substance to exist,’ he told lawmakers. The actor subsequently visited university campuses and rehabilitation centres, speaking out against drug use. Around the same time, he married Polish actress Malgosia Tomassi, whom he had met while filming Hammer. Return to the screen and personal life Keach’s first role after leaving prison was in the CBS television film Intimate Strangers, alongside Teri Garr. It went on to become the third most-watched television film of the 1985–86 season. The Mike Hammer series subsequently returned to television after having been cancelled following his arrest. Years later, Keach played a prison warden in the television series Prison Break (2005–2007). He acknowledged that he had based the character on the real-life governor of the English prison where he had served his sentence, whom he described as compassionate and supportive of efforts to rehabilitate prisoners. Keach was born in Savannah, Georgia, into a family of actors whose parents had met at Northwestern University. He graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, with degrees in English and theatre. He performed at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival, studied at the Yale School of Drama and, as a Fulbright scholar, continued his training at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art. He made his film debut in 1968 in The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter. He worked with John Huston twice, appearing in Fat City and The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean. His other film credits included American History X, alongside Edward Norton, and The Bourne Legacy. His greatest breakthrough, however, remained his portrayal of Mike Hammer – a modern-day knight and defender of the vulnerable. Keach was married four times. He is survived by his wife, Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina. | BGNES
